lines.note: Kyasha describes something clean, refined, and pleasing to look at. This headword repeats the preceding page’s catchword Qiaxa, confirming that the latter is furniture rather than another body entry.
Kyashana has the same sense; kyashana hito applies it to a person. Per begins a metaphorical-use label whose met. is printed on the next row.

runs.text: met. Homem limpo, & aprimorado que ſe cõ-

lines.note: Completes Per met. and describes a neat, well-presented person. The abbreviated cõ- begins the verb concertar across the row break.

runs.text: certa, & atauia bem. ¶ Item, Homem q̃

lines.note: Completes the description of someone who arranges and dresses himself well, then introduces another sense concerning a person’s abilities. The final q̃ is not expanded.
Completes the alternative definition as someone possessing skills and arts. The historical spelling abilidades lacks a written h and is preserved.

runs.text: Dente, ou preſa de porco, elefante,

lines.note: Kiba means a fang or tusk, illustrated by a pig or elephant. The Portuguese preſa refers to the projecting tooth, not captured prey in this context.
Begins a proverb: a lion biting a person does not display its fangs. Xixi is understood as lion from the following Portuguese translation; a- starts the verb arawasazu.
Completes the Japanese negative verb and gives the roman citation label Xix. The Portuguese begins the image of a lion eating a person; homẽ retains its abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: não mostra os dentes. i. O letrado, valente,

lines.note: The lion does not show its teeth; the explanation applies the saying to the learned and the brave. The provisional st typography of mostra is retained.
Completes the proverbial explanation: capable people do not advertise that they are such. This is the dictionary’s interpretation, not a newly supplied Japanese example.
A separate kiba, explained as umanori, means a horseman. The scan has Qiba rather than OCR Qaba, and the explanation marker ends in a comma.
Completes “a man who rides a horse” and gives kiba no shū for mounted people. The Portuguese ends in plain de, without the OCR’s extra nasal tilde.
Completes gente de caualo, mounted men or cavalry. The very short continuation is retained on its own physical row.
Kibamu means becoming yellow. The historical principal form ǒda is visibly printed and is not replaced with a modern nasal past ending; Vo- begins vomote, the face.
Vomote kibamu describes the face turning yellow, directly matched by the Portuguese. The provisional ſt classification in roſto is retained.
Konoha kibamu means tree leaves turning yellow. The omitted paragraph sign is visible at the left, and the Portuguese reads folhas, with h rather than OCR b.
Completes the example as the leaves of trees becoming yellow. Aruores retains the source’s u/v spelling.

runs.text: Caualeiros, ou homẽs que vão a ca

lines.note: Kiba no shū denotes horsemen. The final ca continues into caualo without a visible hyphen; the nasal abbreviation in homẽs is retained.

runs.text: ualo, ou que acompanhão ao ſenhor.

lines.note: Completes caualo and adds men who accompany the lord. The definition concerns a mounted retinue, not merely the animal itself.
Kibarashi is recreation or relief for the heart. The initial Q is part of the headword, not a separate word as suggested by OCR spacing.
Completes the relief-of-the-heart definition. This one-word row belongs to Qibaraxi and is not absorbed into the next entry.

The gloss describes making an effort or exerting oneself to do something more. The scan reads Qbari with no secure i between Q and b, so that printed form is retained rather than silently repaired. The later lexical check identifies kibari/kibaru: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0, lists Qibari; that aid does not override this scan.

runs.text: couſa mais. ¶ Item, per met. Sofrer.

lines.note: Completes “do something more” and adds, metaphorically, enduring or bearing something. The second sense is explicitly marked by per met.
Kibayai describes a hasty or quick-deciding person. The example concerns a prompt response; re- begins reſponder below.
Completes reſponder logo, replying immediately. The line break is preserved inside the Portuguese verb.
Kibi is the grain term glossed as Milho. The scan reads Qibi and Milho, not OCR Qubi and Mulho; the Japanese identifies millet rather than requiring the modern default sense of Portuguese milho.
A separate kibi concerns manner or appearance. Qibi no begins an example in which that manner can be good or bad.
Completes kibi no yoi or warui koto. The Portuguese describes something that looks or presents itself well or badly; l is the Latin alternative marker.
Completes the idiomatic Portuguese description of looking or fitting well or badly. It is the second half of the preceding example’s gloss.
Kibidango are small cakes or dumplings made from kibi. The historical Portuguese Bolinholos is retained, without modernizing its vowels or suffix.
Kibisu and kubisu are alternatives for heel. The false OCR space after Q is removed; the two long-s forms remain as printed.
Kibishii means harsh or severe. The scan supplies i rather than OCR a in the headword, and Qi- begins the example in roman type rather than inside the italic gloss.
Completes kibishii hito, a person with a hard or stern disposition. Con- begins the Portuguese condição below.
Completes condição, the person’s disposition or temperament. No missing additional definition is inferred from this short line.
Kibishisa is the noun for severity or harshness. Its indentation groups the derived form with the preceding adjective.
Kibishū is the adverbial form; yōjin wo kibishū suru means keeping a strict guard. The caron over u and the circumflex in Yôjin are different visible marks.
Translates the example as watching or guarding with great strictness. This is the gloss of the preceding adverbial construction.
Qibo is first glossed as honor. Kore waga ie no qibo nari identifies something as an honor to one’s house; qi- is divided at the row end.

runs.text: Iſto he honra de minha caſa.

lines.note: Completes the Japanese predication and translates it as “this is the honor of my house.” The short-vowel headword is not changed to the following long-vowel homograph.
Adds the sense of benefit or result. Sorega- begins soregaxi, the first-person expression in the following example.

runs.text: xi core made ſanjita qibomo nai.

lines.note: Soregaxi kore made sanjita qibo mo nai complains of having come this far without a worthwhile result. The Portuguese translation begins “I came.”

runs.text: atè qui, & não tenho dißo premio, nem fruito

lines.note: Continues the complaint: having come this far, the speaker has received neither reward nor fruit from it. Enlargement confirms the grave accent in printed atè; dißo and fruito retain their historical spellings.

runs.text: de meu trabalho. ( Isto diz hum quando não

lines.note: Completes “fruit of my labor” and opens a parenthetical explanation of when the phrase is used. The scan has an opening parenthesis, not OCR paragraph sign, and trabalho includes its l.

runs.text: pode alcançar algũa couſa que pretendia. )

lines.note: The phrase is used when someone cannot obtain what he sought. The final closing parenthesis is visible; the false OCR join couſaque is separated.
Kibō is explained as ayauku horoburu, being in danger of destruction. The initial is capital Q, not OCR g; the headword’s caron is retained.
Completes the destruction-risk gloss and gives kibō ni oyobu, reaching such danger. The example repeats Qibǒ, with b rather than OCR o; deſtruir includes the t omitted by OCR.

runs.text: tar, ou chegar ariſco deſe destruir.

lines.note: Completes “be or come to be at risk of destruction.” The compact historical ariſco and deſe, and the provisional st spelling of destruir, are not regularized.

runs.text: Qibǒ. Vyeni nozomu cototo, bǒman ſuru

lines.note: This Qibǒ denotes hunger and satiety; the Japanese paraphrase starts with being hungry and then being full. The headword begins with roman Q, not the OCR’s isolated italic O, and the visible caron is retained.

runs.text: O ter fome, & eſtar farto, & en-

lines.note: Coto completes the Japanese paraphrase. The Portuguese contrasts being hungry with being full, then begins enfastiado across the printed hyphen.
Completes enfastiado, here being satiated or having had enough, rather than introducing a separate headword. The supplied provisional italic st classification is retained.
This second Qibǒ is a respectful address for a religious person, not the hunger-and-satiety entry above. Reuerendo Religioſo introduces its honorific use.

runs.text: que ſe falla honrando a algum Bonzo, ou reli-

lines.note: Explains that the word is used when addressing a bonze or religious person respectfully. The final reli- continues on the next physical row; Bonzo is part of the Portuguese gloss.
Completes religioſo and closes the explanation of the respectful address. No additional Japanese text is printed on this row.

runs.text: Tornar ao primeiro eſtado, ou ſer

lines.note: Qibucu means returning to an earlier state or allegiance. The Portuguese begins restoration to a former condition, completed by the income or dignity below.

runs.text: restituido a ſua renda, ou dignidade. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Restoration can be to one’s revenue or dignity. The paragraph and abbreviated Itẽ open a further sense; the provisional italic st in restituido remains unchanged.

runs.text: Fazer ſe amigo, ou da parte de que era pri-

lines.note: The added sense is becoming a friend or joining the side of someone formerly opposed. Pri- begins primeiro across the physical line break; Fazerſe is not silently substituted for the printed spaced Fazer ſe.
Completes primeiro contrario, then Deusye qibucu xitate- begins the Christian example of returning to God. The printed split is retained rather than recombining the Japanese verb here.
Matçuru completes shitatematsuru from the preceding row. The Portuguese describes a sinner returning to grace; the scan has doubled cc in peccador and a visible continuation indent.
Amizade de Deos completes the restoration to divine grace and friendship. This is the end of the Qibucu example, not another gloss for Qibui.
Qibui is glossed as something harsh or strong. The following short indented forms belong to this adjective rather than representing missing translations.
Qibǔ is the adverbial form associated with Qibui. It is printed alone with a caron over u; the blank remainder of the line is genuine, not omitted Portuguese.
Qibuſa is the corresponding noun of quality, harshness or strength. Like the preceding adverb it is separately indented and has no independent printed Portuguese gloss.
Qibun denotes disposition or bodily condition. Goqibun nanto begins a polite inquiry about a person’s health on the next line.

runs.text: Como eſta voſsa merce de ſaude,

lines.note: Gozaruzo completes go-kibun nanto gozaruzo, asking how the addressee is feeling. The Portuguese similarly asks about health; the worn a in gozaruzo is supported by its remaining type and the construction.
Ou diſpoſição completes the question about health or disposition. The terminal interrogative sign belongs to the Portuguese sentence, not to the next entry.
Qicamafoxij is the older desiderative kikamahoshii, explained by kikitai. Both Japanese forms are roman and have no lexical space after Q; the Portuguese begins wanting to hear.
Completes the gloss with desiring to hear. The final infinitive is printed ouuir, not OCR ouuer; it agrees with ouuir on the previous line.
Qicamafoxiſa is the noun corresponding to the desire to hear. The isolated, indented form has no separate Portuguese gloss, so the blank remainder is preserved.
Qicamafoxǔ supplies the adverbial form of the same desiderative. The initial is roman Q, not an italic O followed by a gap; the visible caron over the final u is retained.
Qican combines hunger and cold, paraphrased by uye and samushi. The glossary’s historical Japanese forms remain roman; the Portuguese gives the same two hardships.
Qicanuo xinogu is enduring hunger and cold. The Portuguese word has an f and reads fome, not ſome; its second object is on the next row.
Frio completes the two hardships endured in the preceding example. The next line begins a distinct compound referring to hunger and thirst.
Qicat is hunger and thirst, glossed in Japanese by uye and cauaqu. Its printed final t is preserved rather than expanded to a modern katsu spelling.
Qicatni voyobu means coming to suffer hunger and thirst. The Portuguese Ter fome, & ſede explicitly confirms both sensations.
Qicatuo yamuru is stopping or satisfying hunger and thirst. Matar a fome begins the corresponding Portuguese idiom; the preceding paragraph introduces this second example.
The sole word ſede completes the idiom for satisfying hunger and thirst. It remains on its own physical continuation row.
Qicaye gives the historical forms of changing clothes, kigae/kikaye. The principal parts yuru and yeta are retained as printed; the Portuguese refers to exchanging garments.
The example first changes horses and then changes armor: uma ni norikaye, yoroi wo kikayete. Restored the clearly printed paragraph sign before the roman Japanese sentence.

The citation is to Taif., book 20, followed by mounting another horse. Enlargement confirms 20 rather than OCR z0, and shows upright Taif. Lib with no printed period after Lib; these citation forms remain roman.
Completes the cited example by putting on different armor. Armas here matches Japanese yoroi rather than referring only to hand-held weapons.
Qicazari is dressing oneself up or adorning oneself in fine clothing. The line ends veſti-, including the i missing in OCR; dos completes the word below.

Dos completes veſtidos, then the Japanese example describes ladies dressing more splendidly in rich brocade. Nhôbǒxu and the printed reôra are retained without modernization; qin- continues into the next row.

The Japanese completes qin-xǔ, rich embroidered or brocaded clothing, as the object of qicazatte. Enlargement shows a u with a worn two-part caron, not the OCR’s o; the Portuguese begins the women dressing themselves.

runs.text: ainda milhor, & ornandoſe de veſtidos ricos,

lines.note: The women dress still better and adorn themselves with rich clothes. The scan reads ornandoſe, not ornandaſe, and the comma after ricos is preserved before the last adjective.
Luſtroſos completes the description of the rich, splendid garments. The entry ends here, before the unrelated color term Qicha.

runs.text: Cor de cha que dão aos veſtidos que

lines.note: Qicha is a tea-related dye color applied to garments, tending toward yellow in the continuation. OCR added an extra s in veſtidos; the printed st-type is represented provisionally as ſt, without a global ligature reclassification.
The dye tends toward yellow. The example contrasts qicha and cobicha; the visible Q begins a single word Qichato rather than being a separate initial.

Completes qicha to cobicha wa sukoshi kawaru: the two colors differ slightly. The supplied ǔa is retained diplomatically, although the mark over u is flattened and may be damaged; it is interpreted as the particle wa, not an asserted long vowel.

runs.text: a cor verde eſcuro tem pouca diſferença.

lines.note: The Portuguese says the yellow-green and dark-green colors differ little. This historical color description is retained as written rather than forced into modern Japanese color categories.
Qichicu is explained by oni and chikushō, a devil and beasts. The final A- starts Animaes in the Portuguese, not a further Japanese form; the printed caron in chicuxǒ is retained.
Nimaes completes Animaes after the capital A- on the previous row. The short continuation belongs to Qichicu and closes that entry.

runs.text: Boa couſa, ou boa ocaßião. Vt,

lines.note: Qichiji is a good event or favorable occasion. The example starts with roman Qi- after italic Vt, not with an italic Japanese fragment or an artificial space inside the word.

Chijiua completes the split Qichijiua; the example invokes the maxim that a good event calls for haste and therefore the reply should also be hurried. The worn iſogu is retained, without supplying an unprinted line-end hyphen.

runs.text: Por quanto ſe diz que a boa

lines.note: Tǒ voriaru closes the quoted statement; enlargement shows a caron rather than a circumflex. The Portuguese reads “because it is said that the good …” and continues with couſa on the next page; there is no terminal bi- or printed hyphen after boa.
The far-right italic catchword repeats the first word of f389, completing boa couſa across the page turn. It is page furniture, not an extra body row.
